recipe.history:
Gouda is one of the oldest continuously produced cheeses in the world, with documentation of its production in the region of South Holland in the Netherlands stretching back to at least 1184 AD — making it one of the few cheeses still being made after more than eight centuries of essentially unbroken tradition. Named for the city of Gouda, which served as a central trading market for the cheese rather than its production site, Gouda was historically made on small family farms throughout the Dutch polders and brought to the Gouda market by boat along the region's intricate canal network. The cheese is a semi-hard to hard washed-curd variety, meaning that during production a portion of the whey is replaced with warm water before pressing, which dilutes the lactose content and produces a milder, sweeter flavor than acid-cured cheeses. Young Gouda, aged only a few weeks to a few months, is mild, buttery, and elastic. Aged Gouda — wheels left to mature for one to three years or more — transforms dramatically: the paste darkens from ivory to deep amber, the texture becomes granular and almost fudge-like, and the flavor develops a profound complexity combining salted caramel, butterscotch, and a crystalline crunch from tyrosine amino acid deposits. Smoked Gouda, a product of Dutch dairy tradition but also of German and American artisan cheesemaking, adds a layer of wood-smoke complexity — typically achieved by cold-smoking young Gouda wheels over hickory, apple, or alder wood — that makes it one of the most versatile and beloved cheeses in any American cheese case.

Gouda arrived in the United States through Dutch colonial settlement in New Amsterdam — present-day New York — as early as the seventeenth century, and Dutch dairy farming traditions influenced the development of American cheesemaking in New York State, Pennsylvania, and the upper Midwest for generations. Smoked Gouda specifically became a popular American deli and specialty cheese item in the 1970s and 1980s, appearing in grocery store cheese departments and gourmet shops as a more interesting alternative to processed American cheese slices. Its application on burgers was natural and rapid: the melting behavior of young smoked Gouda — smooth, creamy, and adhesive — combined with its smoky, mildly sweet flavor profile, makes it a supremely competent burger cheese. It provides smokiness without requiring a smoker, richness without the sharpness of aged cheddar, and an aesthetic visual appeal — its pale yellow paste with its reddish-brown wax coating — that elevates the presentation of any burger it accompanies.

I have been buying smoked Gouda from the same Dutch-owned cheese shop in my city for more than fifteen years. The shop is run by a woman named Hendrika who imports wheels directly from a single cooperative in North Holland, and the Gouda she carries at six months of age has a specific quality I have never been able to fully replicate with any supermarket version: the smoke is deeper and more integrated, having penetrated the rind over months of aging rather than being applied as a surface treatment, and the paste has a gentle give that means it slices cleanly without crumbling. The first time I put a slice of Hendrika's smoked Gouda on a burger patty under a dome of steam, the cheese melted in a single continuous sheet rather than the disconnected pools I had gotten from lesser versions, and the smoke permeated the beef in a way that made the whole patty taste like it had been on a wood-fired grill for hours. The burger was simple — just beef, smoked Gouda, good mustard, and a kaiser roll — but it was one of the best burgers I have made. Some ingredients are not interchangeable.

The Bermuda Triangle pun embedded in this burger's name is a playful reference to mystery and transformation, and indeed the alchemy that happens when a good smoked Gouda is melted over a medium-rare beef patty qualifies as a kind of culinary mystery. At 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C), the beef is juicy and mineral-rich, and the fat is still distributed through the muscle fibers in a way that amplifies rather than muffles the flavor of the Gouda's smoke. When you bite through the melted cheese into that warm, yielding, rosy-centered patty, the smoke and the beef fat and the natural sugars of the cheese all arrive simultaneously, and the result is more than the sum of its parts. This transformation — this disappearance of the individual components into a unified experience — is what the triangle reference is really pointing at. Cook the beef to well done and the triangle closes without you. Medium rare is the only way to be inside the magic.
ingredients: 3 cups bread flour, plus more for kneading
Poppy seeds or sesame seeds, for topping
8 oz smoked Gouda, rind removed, thinly sliced
1 tbsp dark beer or beef broth, to deglaze
Cornichons or bread-and-butter pickles, to serve
instructions: 1. Make the kaiser rolls: Combine the warm water, sugar, and yeast and let bloom 5 minutes. Add the bread flour, salt, and softened butter. Knead in a stand mixer with the dough hook for 9 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Rise in an oiled bowl, covered, for 1 to 1 1/2 hours until doubled. Divide into 4 portions and shape into tight rounds. For the kaiser's characteristic star pattern, use a kaiser roll press or fold and tuck the dough into a five-pointed folded pattern. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and proof 30 to 45 minutes. Brush with beaten egg and sprinkle with poppy or sesame seeds. Bake at 400°F (205°C) for 18 to 20 minutes until deep golden and crisp. Cool on a rack.

2. Make the smoky caramelized onions: Melt the butter with olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-low heat. Add the onions and salt. Cook, stirring every 5 to 8 minutes, for 35 to 40 minutes until very soft and deeply golden. Add the smoked paprika and stir to coat. Add the dark beer or beef broth to deglaze, scraping up any fond from the pan. Cook 2 more minutes. Set aside.

3. Make the beer mustard aioli: Whisk together the mayonnaise, whole-grain mustard, dark beer, honey, apple cider vinegar, and salt until combined and emulsified. Taste, adjust seasoning. Refrigerate until needed.

4. Form the burger patties: Divide the ground beef into 4 equal portions (8 oz / 227g each). Mix the salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Shape the beef gently into patties approximately 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, pressing a dimple in the center of each. Season both sides with the spice mixture immediately before cooking.

5. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook the patties 3 to 4 minutes on the first side without moving. Flip once. Layer the smoked Gouda slices generously over each patty. Cover the pan and add a splash of water to create steam. Cook 2 to 3 more minutes until the internal temperature reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) and the Gouda is fully melted into a smooth, amber-tinged sheet. Rest on a wire rack 3 minutes.
6. Split the kaiser rolls and toast cut-side down in the hot skillet for 60 to 90 seconds until golden and slightly crisp.

7. Assemble: Spread the beer mustard aioli on both bun halves. On the bottom bun, place a leaf of lettuce, then 2 slices of tomato, then a generous pile of smoky caramelized onions. Place the smoked-Gouda-topped patty on top. Cap with the top bun. Serve immediately with cornichons or bread-and-butter pickles on the side.
